entries.name: Art and Literature
entries.content:
ukiyo-e: Ukiyo-e woodblock prints depict everyday life, landscapes, courtesans and kabuki actors.

Kabuki and Bunraku: Kabuki, a theatre that combined dance, drama and music, was one of the most popular forms of entertainment, especially among urban dwellers, while Bunraku is theatre centred on puppets.

Literature: notable works in poetry, such as Matsuo Basho's haiku, and in prose, such as Saikaku's novels, which described the life of merchants and the middle class.

entries.name: Bakutos
entries.content:
Bakuto are groups of people involved in illegal gambling, one of the few "vices" available in a society where other forms of entertainment were highly regulated. These groups operated primarily in underground gambling houses (bakuchi-ba) and organized games of chance such as chō-han and cards.

Bakuto function under a system of hierarchy, with a leader or oyabun (father) directing the members (kobun or sons). This system of semi-feudal relationships is based on loyalty, protection, and respect.

In addition to organizing gambling games, bakuto also lend money at high interest to gamblers, operate pawn shops, and often serve as debt collectors. They take advantage of gamblers who become indebted, and in some cases these debtors will be forced to work for them if they cannot repay their debts.

Bakuto are viewed with contempt by society at large because of their association with gambling, which is considered immoral. Even among criminals, the Bakuto had a low status, and their tattoos were considered a symbol of their marginalization.

entries.name: Board Games
entries.content:
Go: A strategy game of Chinese origin, it was extremely popular among the samurai class and the upper class. It is played on a board with black and white pieces, and the goal is to control more territory than the opponent. It is not only valued as a pastime, but also as a tool to develop strategy and patience.

Shogi: Shogi is a strategy game where players move pieces on a board to capture the opponent's "king." Unlike chess, in Shogi, captured pieces can be reused by the captor, adding an extra layer of complexity. It was very popular among all social classes.

Sugoroku: There are two main forms of sugoroku, an older one called ban-sugoroku (similar to backgammon) and a more recent one called e-sugoroku, a racing game based on the rolling of dice, where players advance around an illustrated board according to the numbers rolled. The latter became popular especially among commoners and children.

Hanafuda and Utagaruta: Hanafuda are Japanese cards with flower illustrations that were used to play various games. Utagaruta, on the other hand, is a card game in which players must match verses from Japanese poems. This game is very traditional and was linked to the appreciation of classical poetry.

entries.name: Climate
entries.content:
Climate zones (
Subtropical forest: In addition, subtropical trees such as bamboo, camphor and wax trees grow in Kyushu, Shikoku and southern Honshu, and the tea plant is cultivated.

Temperate forest: The trees in central and northern Honshu are typical of the temperate zone, such as willows, chestnuts, oaks, birches, elms, lindens and maples.

Boreal forest: Coniferous forests predominate. In Hokkaidō the vegetation is subarctic and similar to that of southern Siberia. Spruce and southern fir are the most common trees, although there are also specimens of alder.
):

Altitudinal zones (

In Japan, mountain forests predominate, which vary according to altitude.

Alpine zone: The alpine climate prevents the growth of trees, but Japanese stone pine and other plants may be present. alpine.
Subalpine zone: Evergreen coniferous forests, especially fir.
Montane zone: Beech, mizunara oak and other deciduous forests.
Piedmont zone: Chinquapin, oak and other evergreen broadleaf forests.

entries.name: Clothes
entries.content:
Clothing in Japan was strongly influenced by social class. Although the kimono is the main garment for men, women and children of all social classes, the quality, materials and styles varied significantly.

Kimono: There are several types of Kimono (

Furisode: A long-sleeved kimono worn by young, unmarried women. It was made of silk and was decorated with bright colours and detailed patterns, indicating the youth and singleness of the wearer.

Kosode: The short-sleeved kimono, worn by married or older women. It was less extravagant than the furisode and was often made of silk or cotton.

Hakama: A garment worn over the kimono, similar to wide, pleated trousers. It is common among samurai men and is also worn at formal ceremonies.

Yukata: A light cotton kimono, worn mainly in summer or after a bath. It was more casual and was worn at festivals or at home.
);


Obi: The obi is a wide sash of strong cloth worn over the kimono. There are several types.

Haori: A short jacket worn over the kimono, common among samurai and wealthy merchants. It is usually made of silk and often has a more sober and masculine design.

Zori: Traditional sandals made of rice straw, wood, leather, or cloth. They were worn with tabi (split socks) and ranged in quality from simple and functional to decorative and luxurious.

Geta: Wooden clogs with a raised base, worn primarily with yukata or in humid climates to keep clothing off the wet ground.







Materials: The materials that clothing is typically made of are (

Silk: Silk is the most luxurious and expensive material, reserved for the samurai class, aristocracy, and wealthy merchants. Silk kimonos are soft, shiny, and often feature intricate hand-dyed or embroidered designs. There are several different types of silk, such as chirimen (a textured silk), habutae (smooth silk), and rinzu (damask silk with woven patterns).

Cotton: Cotton is the most common material for everyday clothing among commoners and peasants. It is more affordable, durable, and easy to wash. Cotton kimonos, known as yukata, are popular during the summer and are worn both as home clothes and at festivals.

Linen: Linen, made from plant fibers such as hemp, is primarily used in the summer due to its lightness and ability to keep the body cool. It is common among the lower classes and in rural areas.

Ramie: Another type of plant fiber, ramie, was used in summer clothing, similar to linen. It was more expensive than cotton, but more affordable than silk. A luxury fabric made with silk threads and sometimes gold or silver, it was used for high-quality and ceremonial kimonos, particularly by the aristocracy.

);

entries.name: Culture and Religion
entries.content:
Neo-Confucianism: Neo-Confucianism became the official state ideology, emphasizing hierarchy, duty, and morality, and reinforcing the rigid social structure of the shogunate.

Buddhism and Shintoism: Some religions like Buddhism provided a framework for spiritual life and death, while Shintoism was more closely tied to national traditions and reverence for nature and kami (spirits).

Samurai Culture: Samurai developed a code of ethics known as bushido (the way of the warrior), which emphasized loyalty, self-reliance, and discipline. Samurai culture also encouraged martial arts and the use of the katana, as well as an education in literary and aesthetic arts.

Popular Culture: Despite strict social divisions, popular culture flourished in cities. Edo, Osaka and Kyoto where various artistic forms such as kabuki theatre, ukiyo-e (woodblock prints) and haiku poetry have emerged.

entries.name: flora and fauna
entries.content:
The flora of Japan is characterized by being extremely lush and varied, this is derived from the climatic diversity of the Japanese archipelago, with a wide range of temperatures and high rainfall, and its humid and warm summers.

In Japan, numerous species of plants with or without flowers can be found, many of them widely cultivated and very popular, such as white and red plum trees, cherry trees, azaleas, peonies, lotuses and, especially, the chrysanthemum, the national flower of Japan.

Other important species are the pimpernel, the bellflower, the gladiolus and many varieties of lilac. There are few wild flowers.

Forests

Almost 70% of Japan's surface is covered by forests. The predominant variety of tree is the conifer. A common species is the sugi, or Japanese cedar. Other notable evergreens are the spruce and many varieties of fir.

The most common fruit trees in Japan are peach, pear and orange trees.

entries.name: Gambling games
entries.content:
Sugoroku: Although in its basic form sugoroku was a family board game, there were versions of the game where money was wagered. Players would bet on what position they would end up in on the board by rolling dice.

Hanafuda: Card games using hanafuda, a type of Japanese card, were often played with bets. Hanafuda games lent themselves well to betting because of their competitive and strategic nature.

Chō-han: This was a simple gambling game that was very popular among ordinary people, particularly men. In the game of chō-han, two dice are rolled into a covered bowl, and players bet on whether the sum of the numbers will be even (chō) or odd (han).

Kendama and Menko: Although these were primarily children's games, sometimes children and teenagers would bet small items or money, especially in the case of menko, where the winner took the opponent's card.

entries.name: Geography
entries.content:
Japan is a geographically complex and diverse country, with a terrain that is mainly characterized by being mountainous. Here are the most relevant characteristics of Japan's terrain:

Mountains are a prominent feature of the Japanese landscape, with many mountain ranges running through the main islands.

Valleys: Valleys are found mainly in mountainous areas and are used for agriculture, especially for the cultivation of rice, which is one of Japan's most important crops.

Volcanoes:
Volcanic activity: Japan is part of the Pacific Ring of Fire, an area known for its high seismic and volcanic activity. The country has more than 100 active and dormant volcanoes. Mount Fuji, although it has not erupted, is still an active volcano.

Coasts:
Irregular coastlines: Japan has a very long and irregular coastline, with many bays, peninsulas and small islands. This gives rise to numerous natural harbors.
Islands: Japan is made up of four main islands (Honshū, Hokkaidō, Kyūshū and Shikoku).

Earthquakes:
Seismicity: Due to its location at the boundary of several tectonic plates, Japan experiences earthquakes regularly, which also influences the type of terrain and the geological formation of the country.

entries.name: kunoichi
entries.content:
Kunoichi are female warriors trained in the arts of stealth, infiltration, intelligence gathering, and assassination. They are employed for covert missions that require skills outside of direct combat, such as espionage, sabotage, and occasionally assassination. However, this does not mean that kunoichi lack combat skills. Unlike samurai, who followed a strict code of honor (bushido), shinobi operated more pragmatically and flexibly, using any means necessary to achieve their goals.

Skills and Techniques: (

Ninjutsu: Shinobi practiced ninjutsu, a set of skills that included stealth, espionage, escape techniques, use of poisons, and unconventional combat. Ninjutsu was not just a martial art, but a set of strategies for surviving and accomplishing missions in hostile conditions.

Weapons: Shinobi used a variety of weapons, some of which were unique to their role, such as the ninjato (a short sword), shuriken (throwing stars), kusarigama (a sickle with a chain), and homemade explosives. They also used tools to climb, disguise themselves, or disorient the enemy, such as the kaginawa (climbing hook) and smoke bombs.

Disguise and Stealth: One of the key techniques of shinobi is the use of disguise and infiltration. They can disguise themselves as peasants, monks or even women to blend in with the population and obtain information without being detected.

All Shinobis are required to learn the "Oppai Concealment" technique to go unnoticed.
);

entries.name: Kyuukyou Temple
Market and economy
entries.content:
Markets (

Ichiba: These were permanent markets set up in larger cities such as Edo, Osaka, and Kyoto. These markets were centers of trade where fresh produce such as rice, fish, vegetables, clothing, utensils, and luxury items were sold.

Rakuichi: These were free markets where merchants could sell their goods without the restrictions normally imposed by guilds. These markets promoted the free movement of goods and competition.

Temple Markets (Ennichi): Many Buddhist temples and Shinto shrines held markets on certain days of the month (known as ennichi). These markets were held on the grounds of temples and shrines and were filled with stalls selling food, amulets, toys, and other goods. They were often associated with religious festivals and attracted large crowds.
):


Economy: (

Agricultural Products: Farmers sold their crops directly at urban markets, making fresh food readily available and varying in season.

Crafts and Consumer Goods: Markets offered a wide range of goods, from kitchen utensils to kimonos, fans, paper, toys, and ceramics. Some markets were specialized, such as those selling tools or books.

Street Food: Markets were famous for their food stalls, where delicacies such as dango (rice balls), yakitori (chicken skewers), taiyaki (fish-shaped cakes), and other typical dishes could be purchased. Street food was a major draw and made markets vibrant and popular places.

Flowers and Bonsai: Flowers, especially in Kyoto markets, were popular, both for decoration and as offerings on altars. Bonsai and other potted plants were also sold and valued for their beauty and cultural significance.
):


Trade: Despite isolation, internal trade is thriving, with the growth of urban markets and a well-developed network of trade routes. Merchants, although at the bottom of the social hierarchy, are gaining considerable economic power, especially in the large cities.

entries.name: Matsuri
entries.content:
Matsuri are traditional festivals held in honor of various deities or to commemorate historical and seasonal events. Each region, city, town, and even shrine had its own festivals, with unique characteristics.

Common Features of Matsuri

Processions (Mikoshi): Many festivals included processions in which a mikoshi (a portable shrine) was carried through the streets, believing that this act brought the blessings of the deities to the community. These processions were vibrant events, with much of the community participating.

Dance and Music: Traditional dances, such as the Bon Odori during the Obon festival, were a central part of many matsuri. In addition, music played on taiko drums, flutes, and other traditional instruments added energy to the festive atmosphere.

Competitions and Parades: At some matsuri, competitions were held, such as races, sumo wrestling, or even poetry contests. Parades with traditional costumes, decorated floats, and theatrical performances were also common.

Fireworks (Hanabi): Fireworks became an important part of many festivals, especially during the summer months. These visual spectacles attracted large crowds and created a festive and joyous atmosphere.


The most important festivals are: (

Gion Matsuri: Held in Kyoto, it features an elaborate procession of richly decorated floats and attracts participants from all over the country.

Sanja Matsuri: Held in the Asakusa district of Edo, this festival is known for its spectacular processions and vibrant energy.

Tenjin Matsuri: Held in Osaka, this festival features processions on land and water, with decorated boats sailing down the river.

Obon: Although more than just a festival, Obon is an important Buddhist tradition held in the summer, where families honor their ancestors. Festivities include the Bon Odori dance and the placing of floating lanterns in rivers and seas to guide spirits back to the other world.

);

Hanami (Flower Viewing): Flower viewing, especially cherry blossoms (sakura), was a popular leisure activity. Families and groups of friends would gather in parks for picnics under the blossoming trees, enjoying nature and each other's company.

entries.name: Politics and society
entries.content:
Social Class: Japanese society was strictly divided into classes, with a rigid hierarchy running from samurai (the warrior class) to peasants, artisans, and merchants. The samurai were the military and bureaucratic elite, and peasants were seen as the most productive class, although they lived under heavy taxes.


Shogunate: The shogunate was a military dictatorship headed by the shogun, the supreme leader, while the emperor held symbolic power and focused on spiritual and cultural issues in Kyoto. The shogun ruled from Edo.


Sakoku: For much of the period, Japan followed a policy of isolation (sakoku), which severely limited trade and outside contact, allowing only controlled trade with China, Korea, and the Netherlands.

Machi-Bugyo: High-ranking officials appointed by the shogunate to govern and administer large cities. Although they had a wide range of administrative and judicial responsibilities, one of their primary duties was to maintain public order and act as judges in criminal and civil cases and oversee public safety and resolve local disputes.

Doshin: Doshin are mid-ranking police officers who worked under the supervision of machi-bugyo. They were responsible for patrolling cities, arresting criminals, and enforcing the law.

Yoriki: Yoriki are higher-ranking officials than doshin and were responsible for overseeing the work of doshin. They often came from the samurai class, and were responsible for coordinating police operations and making sure that the machi-bugyo's orders were carried out correctly.

entries.name: Underwear
entries.content:
Juban: The hadajuban (or simply juban) was a garment of undergarment worn by both men and women. It was a kind of light shirt or robe worn under the kimono to protect it from sweat and direct contact with the skin.
Style and Length: For men, the juban was usually shorter, reaching down to the hip, while for women, it could be longer, sometimes reaching down to the ankles.
Materials: They were commonly made of cotton for everyday wear, but silk versions were popular among the upper classes, especially for special occasions.
Wear by Women: For women, the juban also helped shape the body under the kimono, providing an additional layer that contributed to the flowing silhouette characteristic of the female kimono.

Koshimaki: The koshimaki was a kind of underskirt or petticoat that women wore around the waist, under the juban and kimono. It was similar to a sarong or wrap skirt and provided an additional layer of modesty and protection.

Materials: Like most undergarments, koshimaki was usually made of cotton.

entries.name: Sports
entries.content:
Kyudo (Archery): Archery, especially practiced by samurai, was both a sport and a spiritual discipline. Kyudo required great technical skill and concentration, and was linked to the values ​​of bushido.

Kemari: Kemari is an ancient ball game that has its origins in China, but was popularized in Japan among the nobility. It is a non-competitive game where players pass a ball made of leather, with the goal of not letting it fall to the ground. Although it declined in popularity during this time, it was still practiced in some aristocratic circles.

Kendo: Derived from samurai swordsmanship, kendo is a martial art that simulates combat with bamboo swords (shinai). Although it was more closely related to martial training, it was also practiced as a form of exercise and competition.

entries.name: Samurai
entries.content:
samurai: Samurai emerged as armed servants of the aristocracy, charged with protecting property and maintaining order in an increasingly decentralized feudal Japan. As political power shifted from the imperial court to the feudal lords, the samurai gained influence, becoming a social class of their own. They can be of several types.

hatamoto: The hatamoto are direct vassals of the shogun who enjoy a privileged position within the samurai hierarchy. They are the closest guardians to the shogunate and often held administrative or military leadership roles.

gokenin: Gokenin are hereditary vassals of the shogunate, a class of samurai who served directly under the shogun. This term designated samurai who owned land and swore loyalty to the shogun.

Daimyō: daimyo are feudal lords who ruled large territories and had private armies of samurai. They are the main rivals in feudal politics and key players in the period of civil wars.

ashigaru: Ashigaru are foot soldiers who originally came from the peasant classes.

ronin: ronin are samurai who do not have a lord or daimyo  to serve, usually because their lord had fallen into disgrace or died, leaving his vassals without a fief.

shogun: The shogun is the supreme military leader of Japan and the head of all samurai. Although he serves the emperor, the shogun holds the real power over the country.

entries.name: Yukaku
entries.content:
Yukaku are establishments intended to control and regulate prostitution. They are surrounded by high walls and have guarded entrance gates. By concentrating activities in designated areas, authorities could monitor and tax the industry.

Courtesans and Hierarchy:

Yukaku courtesans were organized in a strict hierarchy. The highest ranking are the oiran, who not only offered sexual services, but also entertained clients with their skills in dance, music, and conversation. The oiran are the bustiest of their profession and therefore their services are extremely expensive and reserved for the wealthiest clients.

Below the oiran were the koshi-joro and the sancha-joro, who also provided entertainment and sexual services, but with less prestige and price.

Finally, at the bottom of the hierarchy were the yujo or lower-ranking prostitutes, whose breasts are usually small so they charge lower rates.

entries.name: Geishas
deities
entries.content: In Japan, two deities representing femininity and oppai are worshipped: Unyuu and Sanyuu. In some areas, they are carved in different shapes, but in general they are usually represented as two young twin women. Unyuu represents the right breast, and Sanyuu the left. Women always pray to bring blessings to their breasts.

entries.name: hats
entries.content:
Various types of hats were used, each with a specific purpose, whether it was for protection from the weather, social status, or even religious beliefs. Below are some of the most representative hats

kasa: General term for traditional Japanese conical hats made of bamboo, straw, or reed. They were used primarily to protect against rain or sun and were common among peasants, travelers, and monks.
  
jingasa: A low, round hat made of leather or iron, often worn by samurai and ashigaru when not in combat. Used to protect against sun and rain while traveling or when not wearing full armor.

takuhatsugasa: A large, conical hat made of bamboo or straw, traditionally worn by mendicant Buddhist monks. Monks wore it while begging, as the size and shape of the hat covered much of the face, symbolizing humility and detachment from the material world.
   
eboshi: A tall, narrow hat made of stiffened silk or lacquered paper typically black worn by Japanese aristocrats and courtiers. It is a key piece of formal attire for the nobility and samurai class. Samurai often wore it under their helmet when in combat.
   
ichimegasa: A conical straw hat, similar to the *amigasa*, but with a looser, less structured design.Worn primarily by upper-class women when traveling, often paired with a veil for privacy.

gauze: A traditional conical straw hat that was worn in different styles and varied by region and social class. It was the generic term for conical hats.It was common among workers and travelers who spent long hours outdoors, protecting themselves from the sun or rain.

kamishimo no Boushi: A hat usually made of stiff cloth or lacquered paper worn by high-ranking samurai and officials during formal ceremonies, often combined with the *kamishimo* outfit. It was mainly worn at formal and ritual events, highlighting the status of the person wearing it.
   
zukin: A type of cloth cap or hood, worn by both men and women. More of a headdress than a hat, it is common among monks, warriors, and pilgrims, and often symbolized humility or religious devotion.


Kanmuri: A ceremonial hat of stiff black cloth or silk, sometimes decorated with ribbons or tassels, worn by nobility and the imperial court during formal rituals. of stiff black cloth or silk, sometimes decorated with ribbons or tassels.

entries.name: swords
entries.content:
Katana: The katana is the most iconic sword and symbol of the samurai warrior. It is a long, curved sword with a single edge, designed for both quick cuts and precise thrusts.

Wakizashi: A shorter sword than the katana, usually carried together, forming the daisho (pair of swords). It is used for combat in close quarters and for seppuku

Tanto: A short knife or dagger, used both as a self-defense weapon and for ceremonial or close combat purposes.

Nodachi: A longer sword than the katana, used by infantry warriors. Due to its size, it was difficult to handle and was usually used in open fields.

entries.name: polearms
entries.content:
naginata: A spear with a long, curved blade at the end, used by both warriors and noblewomen (onnabugeisha) for defense. It was effective at keeping enemies at bay with its long reach.

yari: A straight spear with a sharp blade at the tip. Yari were popular among infantry (ashigaru) due to their versatility in combat, allowing for both thrusts and cuts.

entries.name: blunt weapons
entries.content:
kanabō: A large, heavy club, often made of iron or wood with metal spikes. It was used to strike and break armor or bones, symbolizing brute strength. This weapon is famous in Japanese myths as the tool of demons (oni).

tetsubo: Similar to the kanabō, but made entirely of iron, smaller and more manageable. It was also used to cause blunt force damage to enemies.

entries.name: throwing weapons
entries.content:
shuriken: Throwing stars or small knives used by ninjas (shinobi) and sometimes by samurai as surprise weapons. They were not lethal, but could distract or incapacitate the enemy.

kunai: small, pointed daggers, originally agricultural tools that were also used as throwing or close combat weapons, especially by ninjas.

entries.name: shooting weapons
entries.content:
Yumi: A traditional Japanese longbow, used by both samurai and infantry. The yumi is asymmetrical, being longer at the top, which made it suitable for shooting from a mounted position or on the ground.

Ya: Arrows that accompanied the yumi bow. These arrows could have different tips depending on the purpose, whether it was to pierce armor or cause lethal wounds.

entries.name: unconventional weapons
entries.content:
fukiya: A bamboo tube used to shoot poisoned darts by blowing. It was one of the secret weapons used by ninjas.

makibishi: Small throwing spikes left on the ground to slow down enemies or block their advance. They were used in escape tactics.

tessen: A metal-reinforced war fan. Although it looked like a simple fan, it could be used as a blunt weapon or to deflect sword attacks.

jutte: A small club with a side branch, used by Edo period policemen to disarm criminals without causing lethal harm. It was a key tool for catching and neutralizing criminals.

entries.name: chain weapons
entries.content:
kusarigama: A small sickle attached to a chain with a weight on the end. It was used both to hook and disarm the enemy with the chain and to perform cuts with the sickle.

manriki-gusari: A chain with weights on the ends, used to immobilize or strike opponents. This weapon was commonly used by guards or for self-defense.

entries.name: firearms
entries.content:
tanegashima: Matchlock rifles, although they did not completely replace traditional weapons.

ho: small cannons used in fortifications and in some cases on the battlefield. Their main role is the defense of castles.

entries.name: coins
entries.content:
The monetary system was quite complex and was based on a variety of coins made of different materials: gold, silver, copper and other metals. The value of the coins depended on the material they were made of and their weight.

koban: It is the highest value coin, usually made of pure or almost pure gold used mainly for large transactions and in large-scale trade, such as the purchase of land or important payments.

Ichibuban: Its value was equivalent to a quarter of a *koban* or *ryo*. It was a rectangular coin smaller than the *koban*, and could also be made of silver instead of gold, which affected its value. It was used in important but smaller transactions than those requiring a full *koban*.

Bu: El *bu* equivalía a la mitad de un *ichibuban* o un octavo de un *koban* (1/8 de un *ryo*). Era otra moneda rectangular pequeña, muy utilizada para transacciones medianas.

gin: silver coins were widely used and their value varied depending on weight and purity. Silver coins were very important in international trade and regional exchange. They were used in a wide range of commercial transactions, especially in the payment of taxes and in trade with China and other nations.

Mon
The *mon* was a copper or iron coin, used for more everyday transactions. Its value was much lower compared to gold and silver coins. It was used for small transactions, such as buying food, basic services or everyday products. It was the most common currency for ordinary people, as it was accessible and abundant.

Order from highest to lowest monetary value: 
koban (Gold) 
chibuban (Gold or Silver) 
bu (Gold or Silver) 
gin (Silver Coin)
mon (Copper or Iron)

entries.name: containers
entries.content:
hikifuda: These ropes were used to tie containers or bottles for transport on the back or in wheelbarrows. It was a practical way to secure ceramic or wooden bottles while moving, preventing breakage or spillage.

odawara yoku: These are small wooden barrels made to transport sake or water in larger quantities. They are often used during festivals, celebrations, or for trade. The design of these vessels made them easy to transport by cart or on the shoulder.

hyotan: The hyotan is a dried gourd that was used as a natural water bottle. These gourds were emptied and dried to carry water or sake. They were light and easy to carry, commonly used by travelers, monks, or people on long walks.

take no Suikatsutsu: These are basically bamboo canteens. These are made by cutting and hollowing out sections of bamboo, taking advantage of its tubular shape to store water or tea. These canteens are light and easy to carry on belts or backpacks.


kiseru Bako: Although the kiseru bako is best known for carrying pipes and tobacco, some variants are used to carry small amounts of liquids, such as tea or sake, for personal consumption.

oxen or carts for transporting large quantities:
To transport large quantities of sake or water between villages or within cities, large wooden barrels mounted on carts pulled by oxen or horses were used. These methods were common in rural areas and in markets.

  
inrō : It is a small case that samurai and upper-class men wore hanging from their belt (obi), used mainly to carry small objects such as personal seals, medicines or everyday items.

furoshiki: A square piece of cloth used to wrap and carry objects. The furoshiki is versatile and can be sized to carry anything from clothing to larger items such as packages or books, used by people of all social classes, and could be carried over the shoulder or tied into a bundle.

Fukuro: Simple bags made of cloth or leather. They were used to carry small objects and, depending on the size, could be worn over the shoulder or tied to a belt.
 

Kago: a type of basket or hamper used to transport objects, and in some cases people, although these large baskets were carried by others and were the common method of transporting goods.

Koromo-kago: A basket is a type of basket used to carry clothes or other bulky items. It is made of bamboo or wicker, and was very common among travelers or merchants. It can be carried on the shoulder or on the back, and was an efficient way to transport large amounts of clothes or other items during travel.

Tebako: A small chest or hand box used to carry more valuable items, such as jewelry, documents, or even tea utensils.
